title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Scammers are using AI-powered deepfakes and voice cloning to commit fraud against vulnerable populations in Georgia and South Florida. The attacks include stealing the identity of a real immigration attorney to solicit money from immigrants seeking legal services, and voice cloning in cryptocurrency and grandparent scams. This is impersonation at scale: the deployment of generative AI to create convincing false representations of real people without their consent or knowledge.

The failure occurred where AI systems met no authentication layer. Social media platforms, messaging services, and phone systems accepted deepfaked videos, cloned voices, and spoofed numbers without verification that the person presenting them was genuine. To catch this would have required either the platforms hosting these communications to authenticate the source before delivery, or the targets to have a verification mechanism independent of the content itself, such as a family code word or callback to a known number.

It is not established whether any particular AI company built these deepfake or voice-cloning systems, or whether the criminals used commercial tools, open-source models, or custom systems.

summary:
Scammers are increasingly using artificial intelligence technology to commit fraud in Georgia and South Florida by creating deepfakes and cloning voices. Recent cases include a South Florida immigration attorney whose identity was stolen to target vulnerable immigrants, and a Cobb County couple who lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans reported nearly $893 million in AI-enabled scam losses last year. Florida experienced 350 AI-related complaints totaling $39.9 million in losses, while Georgia reported 71 complaints with $10.4 million in losses.

Criminals use AI to make traditional scams more convincing by cloning voices from social media, spoofing phone numbers, creating fake photos, and researching victims' personal relationships. Common schemes include the grandparent scam, romance scams, and emergency requests. Federal investigators warn that these figures likely underestimate the actual problem since many victims never report being scammed. Authorities recommend establishing code words with family members, verifying urgent requests through known phone numbers, and avoiding immediate responses to unexpected requests for money or sensitive information.
